cases.title: Karimenu II dam: land taken in Gatundu North and compensation still unpaid
cases.place: Kiriko, Gituamba ward, Gatundu North, Kiambu County, Kenya
cases.point: The Karimenu II dam in Gituamba ward, Gatundu North (OpenStreetMap, found through Nominatim). AidData's own coordinate for this record points to a village called Kiriko outside Gatundu North.

lenders.name: China Eximbank
lenders.role: AidData record 58737. A US$200,530,600 loan signed on 14 February 2017 to the AVIC & SMEDI joint venture, financing 85 per cent of a US$235,918,461 engineering, procurement, construction and financing contract; final maturity 21 July 2042, repayable in 20 equal half-yearly instalments. Disbursements of US$13,364,912 in Kenya's 2020-21 financial year and US$133,093,268 in 2021-22; US$158,254,011 outstanding at 30 June 2022. This is not a World Bank project and has no P-number.

cases.conditions: The loan went to the Chinese contractor rather than to the state: China Eximbank lent to the AVIC & SMEDI joint venture to cover 85 per cent of its own contract, with what AidData records as an apparent repayment guarantee from the Government of Kenya (AidData record 58737).

companies.name: AVIC International Holding Corporation
companies.role: Lead of the joint venture that held the engineering, procurement, construction and financing contract signed 24 April 2017 (AidData record 58737; The Star)

companies.name: Shanghai Municipal Engineering Design Institute (Group) Co., Ltd
companies.role: Joint venture partner on the same contract, responsible for design (AidData record 58737)

companies.name: Athi Water Works Development Agency
companies.role: Kenyan state water agency under the Ministry of Water and Sanitation that signed the contract and implemented the works; AidData's record names it in its earlier form, Athi Water Services Board

cases.community: The works needed 600 acres: 171 acres in the first phase for the dam embankment and water draw-off structures, and 429 acres in the second phase for the reservoir area (AidData record 58737). On 1 August 2019 the water cabinet secretary Simon Chelugui said 246 affected people had been paid Sh1.28 billion for 171.6 acres in phase one, and that valuation of phase two had only just been finished; residents said they would block the project until phase two was paid. Jackson Mbugua said phase one compensation had started in 2017 and was only finalised in 2019, and that they feared phase two would be paid after the dam was built. Zipporah Wanjiru said: "If they want us to allow them to continue, let them pay us our money. We are not against the project" (The Star, 1 August 2019). On 26 February 2020 the implementing agency said 228 of the 246 phase one claimants had been paid Sh1.09 billion and 28 were still unpaid - 18 of the original claimants and 10 more who arose from subdivided plots - so the contractor had access to 136.5 of the 171 acres, and that the 34.5 acres left out were the ones needed for the diversion tunnel, intake tower and bridge (The Star, 26 February 2020). On 20 September 2023 Kiambu senator Karungo Thang'wa said 150 acres at Kianjuku in Gatundu North were affected by constant backflow from the finished dam, and that residents were suffering instead of benefiting (The Star, 20 September 2023). On 13 September 2025 the agency's chief executive Joseph Kamau said people in the buffer zone, about 50 metres above the top water line, had still not been paid: "We have compensated where the water sits, but we have not compensated an area we usually call the buffer zone." He said the valuation had gone to the National Land Commission and he expected movement by October, and conceded the process was behind schedule. Simon Nguyai Timothy, one of those waiting, said he had come hoping the water minister would address the compensation and was disappointed. In September 2023 President William Ruto had directed the then water minister Alice Wahome to settle Sh4.2 billion owed to affected families (Capital FM, 13 September 2025).
cases.outcome: The dam was completed and commissioned in August 2022 (Capital FM, 13 September 2025). Compensation for the buffer zone around the reservoir was still unpaid in September 2025, with the valuation lodged with the National Land Commission (Capital FM).

cases.confidence_note: Two Kenyan news organisations and the implementing agency's own statements carry the unpaid compensation, so the harm does not rest on the lender's account. Two phase-one payment figures differ and both are given here: the water cabinet secretary said Sh1.28 billion to 246 people on 1 August 2019, and the agency said Sh1.09 billion to 228 people on 26 February 2020. AidData's record is the only source here carrying the figure of 383 acres surrendered for phase two and still unpaid in early 2021. AidData also notes that two other databases give different face values for the same loan - SAIS-CARI US$31 million and Boston University US$229 million - and that it follows the US$200,530,600 recorded in Kenya's external public debt register.
cx: Karimenu II dam land acquisition and compensation
cases.ecosystem: The dam is 59 metres high and holds 26.5 million cubic metres on the Karimenu river, below its meeting with the Gathanje, Kagundu and Githanga streams (AidData record 58737). The senator for Kiambu reported 150 acres at Kianjuku affected by backflow from the reservoir (The Star, 20 September 2023).
cases.whole: The dam supplies 70 million litres of water a day to Juja, Ruiru and parts of Nairobi, which Capital FM reports as serving nearly one million people. In February 2020 more than 500 local residents had jobs at the site as casual workers, machine operators, drivers and technicians; casuals earning Sh498 a day asked for Sh700, and excavator operators earning Sh1,000 asked for Sh2,000, one driver saying they were still being paid at 2013 rates (The Star, 26 February 2020).

cases.title: Lamu coal plant: land taken at Kwasasi and never paid for
cases.place: Kwasasi, Hindi division, Lamu County, Kenya
cases.point: The plant site at Kwasasi, about 21 km north of Lamu town, from the coordinates given in AidData's record (02 09 13 S, 40 54 12 E).

lenders.name: Industrial and Commercial Bank of China (ICBC)
lenders.role: AidData record 52499. Indicative term sheet for a US$900 million export credit signed with Amu Power Company Limited on 8 June 2015: 18-year maturity, four-year grace period, three-month LIBOR plus a 2 per cent margin, a 1.1 per cent arrangement fee, a 0.8 per cent commitment fee and a 2 per cent default rate, with buyer's credit insurance from Sinosure and project revenues, project assets and the Sinosure policy pledged as security. AidData records the financing as cancelled. The Star reported ICBC was to put in US$1.2 billion, 60 per cent of the US$2 billion cost. No World Bank P-number: this is not a World Bank project.

lenders.name: African Development Bank
lenders.role: Was expected to provide a partial risk guarantee and announced on 24 November 2019 that it was leaving the project (AidData record 52499); The Star reported the bank retreated citing plans to divest from coal.

lenders.name: Standard Bank Group
lenders.role: Had concluded debt financing agreements with ICBC and the Kenyan investors, according to the bank's own 2015 annual integrated report as cited by AidData; The Star reported it reversed a US$300 million investment decision in 2017.

cases.conditions: An export credit tied to Chinese supply, insured by Sinosure, with the project's revenues and assets pledged as security (AidData record 52499).

companies.name: Amu Power Company Limited
companies.role: Project company set up to build, own and operate the plant and sell power to Kenya Power and Lighting Company under a 25-year agreement; a joint venture of Kenya's Centum Investment and Oman's Gulf Energy (AidData record 52499; The Star)

companies.name: Power Construction Corporation of China
companies.role: Engineering, procurement and construction contractor named for the project (AidData record 52499)

companies.name: Sichuan Electric Power Design and Consulting Company Limited
companies.role: Engineering, procurement and construction contractor named for the project (AidData record 52499)

companies.name: General Electric
companies.role: Signed a Sh50 billion agreement with Amu Power to design, build and maintain the plant and to take a stake later; left the project in September 2019 saying it was exiting coal power (The Star, 18 November 2020)

cases.community: At least 975 acres at Kwasasi village in Hindi division were acquired in 2016 for the plant, and by August 2020 the owners had still not been paid. Their spokesman Hussein Fadhil said: "We surrendered our land and moved out thinking the project would take off shortly after and enable us receive our compensation but that has not been the case. As it is, we have no idea if the project will ever happen. We need our land back." Mohamed Omar said some of them had no other land and had been renting since 2016. The National Land Commission's review had set an acre at Sh800,000 (The Star, 11 August 2020). In July 2018 members of the Kwasasi Farmers Association demonstrated in Lamu, saying they had given up 1,000 acres and had been waiting five years; their chairman Abdul Rahman Aboud demonstrated in support of the plant and against the conservation groups opposing it, while asking the government to speed up payment. The land commission chairman Muhammad Swazuri said the farmers would soon be paid Sh800,000 an acre, and the farmers said that was not enough (The Standard, 9 July 2018). AidData's record quotes Save Lamu and the Kwasasi Mvunjeni Farmers Self-Help Group, which opposed the plant, saying "our farmers are being displaced from their land, losing their income and food security, without a clear plan for their compensation" and that artisanal fishing and tourism faced threats from the plant.
cases.outcome: Construction never started. Kenya's National Environment Tribunal revoked the plant's environmental licence in June 2019 for inadequate public participation and ordered a new assessment, and Amu Power appealed (The Star, 18 November 2020; AidData's record dates the ruling 26 July 2019). Save Lamu announced on 16 November 2020 that ICBC had pulled out, citing a bank official; ICBC made no public announcement and did not answer The Star's questions, and a press attache at the Chinese embassy in Nairobi, Shelly Huang, said: "I never heard ICBC has intention or interests in investing in the proposed coal project. My information is that the project has been suspended since several years ago. Not a single Chinese company is involved in it now" (The Star, 18 November 2020). The landowners were asking for their land back (The Star, 11 August 2020).

sources.title: AidData record 52499: [Cancelled] ICBC provides $900 million export credit for 981.5 MW Lamu Coal-Fired Power Plant Project
Lamu residents want land back over delayed compensation
Farmers demand pay for their land
Lamu coal plant's biggest investor abandons project

cases.confidence_note: The land acquisition and the non-payment are carried by two Kenyan newspapers quoting the landowners and the National Land Commission, not by the lender. The acreage differs between them: 975 acres acquired in 2016 (The Star, 11 August 2020) and 1,000 acres (The Standard, 9 July 2018). The link to this lender is contested: ICBC never confirmed the credit publicly, the withdrawal was announced by Save Lamu rather than by the bank, the Chinese embassy in Nairobi said no Chinese company was involved in the project, and AidData records the export credit as cancelled with an unknown commitment date. AidData gives the plant as 981.5 MW while the Kenyan reports give 1,050 MW.
cx: Lamu coal plant land acquisition and the cancelled ICBC export credit
cases.ecosystem: The site covers about 395 hectares in the Kwasasi area north of Lamu town (AidData record 52499). Save Lamu, an umbrella body of more than 40 Lamu organisations, objected that the plant put the health, livelihoods, food security, environment and cultural heritage of the area at risk, and that artisanal fishing and tourism depended on the marine environment it would disturb (AidData record 52499).
cases.whole: No power was ever generated. The plant would have been Kenya's first coal-fired station and the largest in East Africa, burning coal imported from South Africa at first and later coal from the Mui Basin in Kitui County, with power carried to Nairobi on a new 520 km, 400 kV line (AidData record 52499; The Star, 11 August 2020). Amu Power's chairman of the local farmers' association said the project would give jobs to about 3,000 young people (The Standard, 9 July 2018); AidData's record says about 3,000 workers were expected on site, 1,400 of them Chinese.

cases.title: Addis Ababa-Djibouti railway: farmland taken and compensation paid at unequal rates
cases.place: The Ethiopian section of the railway, from Sebeta to the Djibouti border, Ethiopia
cases.point: Mieso (Mi'eessoo), West Hararghe, where the two Chinese-built sections of the line meet (OpenStreetMap, found through Nominatim). The compensation complaints were spread along the Ethiopian section and the documents do not name the kebeles.

lenders.name: China Eximbank
lenders.role: AidData records 70086, 70085, 70083 and 46183. A single buyer's credit of US$2,490,760,000 signed with the Government of Ethiopia on 15 May 2013, at 15-year maturity, six-year grace and LIBOR plus 3 per cent, insured by Sinosure, drawn in three tranches: US$1,289,029,000 for the 329 km Sebeta-Adama-Meiso section (record 70086), US$981,260,000 for the 339 km Meiso-Dewanle section (record 70085) and US$220,471,000 for rolling stock (record 70083). A separate US$491,793,000 buyer's credit went to the Government of Djibouti for the 100 km Ali Sabieh to Nagad section (record 46183). This is not a World Bank project and has no P-number.

cases.conditions: The Ethiopian authorities secured the package on condition that Chinese railway technology and Chinese contractors were used (The People's Map of Global China). Each tranche covered 70 to 85 per cent of a commercial contract with a Chinese state firm (AidData record 70086).

companies.name: China Railway Engineering Corporation (CREC)
companies.role: Held the US$1,841,470,000 engineering, procurement and construction contract for the 329 km Sebeta to Mieso section, signed 25 October 2011 (AidData record 70086)

companies.name: China Civil Engineering Construction Corporation (CCECC)
companies.role: Held the US$1,401,800,000 contract for the 339 km Mieso to Dewelle section, signed 16 December 2011, and built the Djibouti section (AidData record 70086; The People's Map of Global China)

companies.name: China North Industries Corporation (NORINCO)
companies.role: Held the US$259 million rolling stock contract signed in March 2013 (AidData record 70086)

companies.name: Ethiopian Railway Corporation
companies.role: Ethiopian state corporation that owned the project and paid the compensation through its Right of Way and Compensation Department (AidData record 70086; The Reporter)

cases.community: Ethiopia's parliament took up the compensation after its members visited claimants. The Reporter wrote on 31 March 2018 that the Public Enterprises Standing Committee of the House of People's Representatives had questioned the Ethiopian Railway Corporation over varying compensation payments and the handling of farmers' claims on the Ethio-Djibouti line. Members said several farmers had not been compensated although their farmland had been damaged, that thousands of farmers had complained of unfair treatment, that some received more and others less for the same plot, that some were paid nothing while their neighbours were paid, and that the corporation paid farmers who threatened it while poorer claimants were refused. One member said: "After their farmlands are taken away, most farmers have been forced to go to the streets while some suffer from lack of finance for medical treatment," and described a woman with cancer whose land had been taken for a development project. The head of the corporation's Right of Way and Compensation Department, Fadil Ibrahim, confirmed to the committee that there had been unequal payments for similar farmland, citing two kebeles where one was paid 25 birr a square metre and the other up to 300 birr a square metre. He said the corporation paid the rate the local administrations valued: "We are not the organization to blame for the delay of compensation. We pay, when the wereda administrations present the compensation rate. It is not our mandate to carryout valuation" (The Reporter, 31 March 2018). A profile of the line written by Yunnan Chen for The People's Map of Global China says rural landowners were displaced by the construction and that compensation was set by the state, which owns all land in Ethiopia, and that the route runs through Oromia where tensions have centred on land displacement.
cases.killed_note: The railway corporation paid compensation above market price for camels and other livestock killed in collisions on the track, which is unfenced at its own request (AidData record 70086; The People's Map of Global China). No death of a person is recorded in these sources.
cases.outcome: The line opened to passengers on 4 October 2016, was handed over to its builders' operating consortium on 31 December 2017 and began commercial operations on 1 January 2018 (AidData record 70086). The compensation claims were still unresolved when parliament examined them in 2018 (The Reporter). Ethiopia deferred repayment in 2018 and agreed a 20-year maturity extension and a four-year grace extension with China Eximbank; Djibouti's loan was restructured by an agreement signed on 2 September 2020 and ratified into Djiboutian law in February 2021 (AidData records 70086 and 46183).

sources.title: ERC grilled over capricious, delayed compensation for farmers
AidData record 70086: China Eximbank provides $1.28 billion buyer's credit loan for Sebeta-Adama-Meiso Section of Addis Ababa-Djibouti Railway Project
Addis-Djibouti Railway (project profile by Yunnan Chen, updated 8 April 2021)
sources.publisher: The People's Map of Global China

cases.confidence_note: The compensation findings rest on one newspaper report of a parliamentary hearing, in which the railway corporation's own department head confirmed the unequal payments and named the two rates. No source gives a count of the people or households moved, and the two kebeles he compared are not named. The People's Map profile, written by a researcher at the Overseas Development Institute, records displacement of rural landowners without a figure.
cases.whole: The 759 km line is the first cross-border standard gauge railway and the first fully electrified railway in Africa, and the only rail link between landlocked Ethiopia and the port of Djibouti (The People's Map of Global China; AidData record 70086). Traffic came in below the forecast the debt was built on: the passenger fare was cut from 30 birr to 4 birr, most freight has been imports rather than exports, power surges and flooding halted services in the first year, Sinosure reportedly wrote off US$1 billion on the line's performance, and Ethiopia deferred repayment in 2018 (AidData record 70086; The People's Map of Global China).

lenders_add.name: China Eximbank
lenders_add.role: AidData records 45520 and 95928. Two buyer's credit loans signed with the Government of Sri Lanka on 17 February 2011 for Section IV of the expressway, Pinnaduwa to Godagama: US$74,329,906 under agreement BLA201011 for Package 1 (km 30.8 to 45) and US$55,369,520 under agreement BLA201012 for Package 2 (km 45 to 61.05 plus remaining work on the Galle port access road). Both carried six-month LIBOR plus a 2.40 per cent margin, a 15-year maturity, a four-year grace period, a 0.7 per cent commitment fee, a 0.3 per cent management fee and a 6 per cent Sinosure premium. Sri Lanka's pre-emptive default announced on 12 April 2022 suspended payments on China Eximbank loans then outstanding.

sources_add.title: AidData record 45520: China Eximbank provides $74.3 million buyer's credit loan for Package 1 of Section IV (Pinnaduwa-Godagama) of Southern Transport Development Project

fields_add.conditions: China Eximbank financed Section IV of the expressway, from Pinnaduwa to Godagama, under two buyer's credit loans signed in February 2011. China National Technical Import & Export Corporation held the engineering, procurement and construction contract for both packages, signed on 11 June 2010, started work in April 2011 and finished in January 2014; that section opened to traffic on 16 March 2014 (AidData records 45520 and 95928).
fields_add.confidence_note: The displacement findings here come from the Compliance Review Panel's review of the Asian Development Bank's loan. China Eximbank's two loans came later, in 2011, and paid for Section IV from Pinnaduwa to Godagama; no harm on that section is recorded in AidData's records of those two loans.

lenders_add.name: China National Petroleum Corporation
lenders_add.role: AidData record 34197. This Chinese state-owned company pledged US$32 million in 2013, recorded by AidData as a grant with a commitment date of 1 January 2013, to compensate farmers whose land was taken for the pipelines and the railway works built for them. AidData says whether the pledged sum was delivered is unclear.

sources_add.title: AidData record 34197: CNPC pledges 32 million USD to compensate farmers in response to pipeline projects
Rakhine Residents Issue Demands for Pipeline Compensation
Myanmar Jails Activists Over Protest Against China-Led Petroleum Project
sources_add.publisher: Radio Free Asia, via ecoi.net (document 1268827, published 26 September 2013)

sources_add.title: Farmers Demand Compensation for Farmland Destroyed by Gas Pipeline

fields_add.community: China National Petroleum Corporation pledged US$32 million in 2013 to compensate farmers displaced by the works. AidData's record says local officials reported residents were paid in full at 4 million kyat, about US$4,625, for each hectare of land lost, that some residents said they received nothing, and that a CNPC official said compensating former landowners was difficult because most land on Maday Island was registered as vacant and most residents had no ownership documents; AidData is the only source here carrying those figures and says it is unclear whether the pledge was paid. On 2 August 2013 representatives of 30 villages delivered a list of demands to township, district and party offices in Kyaukpyu, asking for schools, clinics, roads between the villages, drinking water and electricity as compensation for the pipeline; Maung Aye of their Local Development Committee said they asked for an answer within 15 days, and officials of the pipeline's operators refused to accept the letter, saying it was a matter for local authorities. About 400 people had protested in April 2013 saying they were inadequately compensated for their land (Radio Free Asia, 2 August 2013). On 19 February 2015 fifty farmers from 12 villages in Kyaukpyu township demonstrated outside the township administration office over farmland buried in mud by the pipeline construction and not paid for. One, U San Shwe, said they had claimed three times already. Farmers whose land was covered in mud had been paid in September 2013 and a Chinese gas company had paid 385,000 kyat an acre of mud-covered paddy, but nothing had been paid for that season's crop. U Wai Dawn of Pyar-Tae village said: "We are being squeezed between the company and the government" (Narinjara, 24 February 2015).
fields_add.suppression: On 19 April 2013 authorities in Kyaukpyu charged six villagers, said to be organisers of the protest held the day before, with illegal assembly for marching without a permit; the villagers had applied for permits in December at township and state level and were refused both times, and a number of Maday Island residents who worked as labourers for CNPC were dismissed after the protest (Radio Free Asia, 2 August 2013). Radio Free Asia reported on 26 September 2013 that a court in Kyaukpyu township had jailed ten people for three months each under Article 18 of the Peaceful Assembly Law over the same march. About 300 people from 20 villages gathered at the court demanding their release; one, Ko Nyi Nge, said that if the ten were not freed the authorities should arrest all the villagers who had protested. About 100 security force members and several firefighters ringed the court but did not act. Their lawyer Htein Lin said no witness testified that the ten had led the protest and said he would appeal. Human Rights Watch's deputy Asia director Phil Robertson said: "By jailing peaceful protesters, the Burmese government is creating a new class of political prisoners."
fields_add.confidence_note: The arrests, the jail sentences and the dismissal of CNPC labourers after the April 2013 protest are reported by Radio Free Asia, and the February 2015 protest over mud-damaged farmland by Narinjara. The US$32 million pledge and the 4 million kyat a hectare rate are carried only by AidData's record, which says it is unclear whether the pledge was delivered.
